property_summary: For any caller who is the current owner, calling NETM preserves that caller's balance as equal to totalDistributed (i.e., balances[owner] == totalDistributed); the mutant that sets owner = address(0) breaks this because balances[oldOwner] no longer equals balances[owner] (owner becomes zero address) so the invariant can fail for some inputs.

For any caller x, invoking NETM() on the correct contract preserves that owner’s balance equals totalDistributed (i.e., balances[owner] == totalDistributed) after the call; the mutant that omits crediting balances breaks this (some owner addresses will have balances[owner] != totalDistributed).

For any caller who is the owner, calling NETM() resets owner to msg.sender and also (in the reference) ensures balances[owner] equals totalDistributed; the mutant that omits crediting the owner's balance can make balances[owner] != totalDistributed after NETM, so the property is that balances[ c.owner() ] == c.totalDistributed() always holds after NETM is called by the owner.

After calling NETM() by the owner, the reference contract always sets balances[newOwner] == totalDistributed and owner == msg.sender, but the mutant writes balances for the previous owner instead, so there exists inputs where balances at some address (the new owner) differs between reference and mutant.

For any caller who is the contract owner and invokes NETM(), the reference contract always sets balances[owner_after_call] == totalDistributed; the mutant may instead set balances for the previous owner, so there exist owner values where balances[owner_after_call] != totalDistributed.
